items.readable_text:
Content:
In a previous lesson, we learned that given two paired samples of size [MATH: n{:}]

Content:
[MATH: X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n, \qquad Y_1, Y_2, \ldots, Y_n,]

Content:
we can reduce this to a set of single-sample observations by defining the difference between each observation as

Content:
[MATH: D_i = X_i - Y_i.]

Content:
If we assume that the differences are independent and identically distributed (I.I.D), then we have two cases:

Content:
- If each [MATH: D_i] is normally distributed, then the distribution of the sample mean [MATH: \overline D] is given by
[MATH: \overline{D} \sim N\left(\mu, \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}\right)]
where [MATH: \mu] is the population mean of [MATH: D_i,] and [MATH: \sigma^2] is the population variance of [MATH: D_i.]
- If each [MATH: D_i] is not normally distributed but the sample size is large, then by the central limit theorem,
[MATH: \overline{D} \approx N\left(\mu, \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}\right).]

Content:
In either case, we can construct a [MATH: [100(1-\alpha)]\%] confidence interval for [MATH: \mu] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \overline{d} \pm z_{\alpha/2}\cdot\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}]

Content:
where

Content:
- [MATH: \overline{d}=\overline{x}-\overline{y}\,] is a point estimate for [MATH: \mu,]
- [MATH: P(Z > z_{\alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2}] and [MATH: Z\sim N(0,1).]

Content:
In most practical situations, [MATH: \sigma^2] is unknown, so we must use the sample variance [MATH: S^2.] This introduces additional variability, and the resulting random variable:

Content:
[MATH: T = \dfrac{\overline D - \mu}{S/\sqrt n}]

Content:
follows a [MATH: t]-distribution with [MATH: n-1] degrees of freedom. This is exact if [MATH: D_i] is normally distributed and approximate in the large sample case.

Content:
Thus, our confidence interval is given by

Content:
[MATH: \overline{d} \pm t_{n-1, \alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}]

Content:
where

Content:
- [MATH: s^2] is the sample variance, and
- [MATH: P(T > t_{n-1, \alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2}.]

Content:
Let's see some examples.

sections.normalized_html:
We do not know the distribution of the difference [MATH: D,] nor do we know the population variance [MATH: \sigma^2.] However, the sample size [MATH: n = 150\geq 30] is sufficiently large.

In cases like this, the random variable

[MATH: \dfrac{\overline{D} - \mu}{S/\sqrt n}]

can be approximated by the student's [MATH: t]-distribution [MATH: T_{n-1}] with [MATH: n-1] degrees of freedom, where

where

  • [MATH: \overline{D}] is the sample mean of the differences,

  • [MATH: \mu] is the population mean of the variable [MATH: D,]

  • [MATH: S^2] is the sample variance of the differences, and

  • [MATH: n] is the sample size.

Given a value [MATH: \alpha] between [MATH: 0] and [MATH: 1,] the corresponding [MATH: [100(1-\alpha)]\%] confidence interval for the population mean [MATH: \mu] is given by

[MATH: \overline{d} \pm t_{n-1,\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}},]

where

  • [MATH: P(T > t_{n-1,\alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2},] and [MATH: T] has a student's [MATH: t]-distribution with [MATH: n-1] degrees of freedom,

  • [MATH: \overline{d}] is a point estimate of [MATH: \mu,]

  • [MATH: s] is an unbiased estimate of [MATH: \sigma,] the standard deviation of [MATH: D.]

In our case,

[MATH: \overline{d}=5.6, \qquad n = 150, \qquad s = 2.]

We are interested in finding a [MATH: 99\%] confidence interval. So, we have

[MATH: \alpha=1-0.99=0.01 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \dfrac{\alpha}{2}=0.005.]

From the table, we can see that [MATH: P(T_{149} > 2.609) = 0.005.] As a result,

[MATH: t_{n-1,\alpha/2} = t_{149,0.005} = 2.609,] as shown below.

Therefore, the [MATH: 99\%] confidence interval for the population mean [MATH: \mu] of the difference is the following:

[MATH: 5.6|± 2.609 ⋅ (2)/(sqrt(150))] which approximately equals [MATH: 5.6|± 0.4.]

Let us call [MATH: D] the random variable representing the difference in the number of students attending a randomly selected course at locations A and B.

[MATH: \dfrac{\overline{D} - \mu}{S/\sqrt n}]

[MATH: \overline{d} \pm t_{n-1,\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}},]

[MATH: \alpha=1-0.98=0.02 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \dfrac{\alpha}{2}=0.01,]

We are given that [MATH: P(T_{33} > 2.445) = 0.01.] As a result,

[MATH: 1.20|± 2.445 ⋅ (4)/(sqrt(34))]

[MATH: 1.20|± 1.68.]

Content:
[MATH: X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n, \qquad Y_1, Y_2, \ldots, Y_n,]

Content:
we can reduce this to a set of single-sample observations by defining the difference between each observation as

Content:
[MATH: D_i = X_i - Y_i.]

Content:
If we assume that the differences are independent and identically distributed (I.I.D), then we have two cases:

Content:
- If each [MATH: D_i] is normally distributed, then the distribution of the sample mean [MATH: \overline D] is given by
[MATH: \overline{D} \sim N\left(\mu, \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}\right)]
where [MATH: \mu] is the population mean of [MATH: D_i,] and [MATH: \sigma^2] is the population variance of [MATH: D_i.]
- If each [MATH: D_i] is not normally distributed but the sample size is large, then by the central limit theorem,
[MATH: \overline{D} \approx N\left(\mu, \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}\right).]

where

- [MATH: P(Z > z_{\alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2}] and [MATH: Z\sim N(0,1).]

where

- [MATH: s^2] is the sample variance, and
